recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows MACS J1149.5+2223, a huge cluster of galaxies. The light we see from it set out more than 5 billion years ago, so the picture shows the cluster as it was in the distant past.

A galaxy cluster is a vast gathering of galaxies bound together by gravity, and its enormous mass warps the space around it. Light from objects far behind the cluster is bent as it passes through, a process called gravitational lensing.

Here the lensing does two things. It magnifies and distorts the light of more distant galaxies, stretching them into unfamiliar shapes. And it can split the light of a single distant object along several paths, so that the same background source appears more than once in the image. For astronomers, a lens like this acts as a natural telescope, bringing faint, far-off galaxies into view that would otherwise be too dim to study.
scale: Light from the cluster took over 5 billion years to reach us, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: This image combines near-infrared light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The filters used record near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the long exposures reveal galaxies far too faint to see by eye.
